question: What type of trailer is especially prone to getting stuck on raised railroad crossings due to low underneath clearance?
choice_a: A low-slung unit such as a lowboy, car carrier, moving van, or possum-belly livestock trailer
choice_b: A flatbed trailer hauling lumber
choice_c: A standard dry van trailer
choice_d: A tanker trailer hauling fuel
explanation: The manual specifically warns that low slung units like lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, and possum-belly livestock trailers can get stuck on raised railroad crossings.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Railroad-Highway Crossings

question: If your combination vehicle gets stuck on railroad tracks, what should you do first?
choice_a: Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then call 911 or another emergency number
choice_b: Try to drive forward at full throttle to clear the tracks
choice_c: Stay in the vehicle and honk the horn continuously
choice_d: Uncouple the trailer and leave the tractor on the tracks
explanation: The manual instructs that if you get stuck on the tracks, get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then call 911 or another emergency number and give the crossing's location using landmarks or the DOT number.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Railroad-Highway Crossings

question: What is the earliest and best way to recognize that a trailer has started to skid?
choice_a: Seeing it in your mirrors
choice_b: Feeling the steering wheel vibrate
choice_c: Hearing the tires squeal
choice_d: Watching the speedometer drop suddenly
explanation: The manual states the earliest and best way to recognize a trailer skid is by seeing it in your mirrors, especially any time you apply the brakes hard.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Prevent Trailer Skids

question: When a trailer's wheels lock up and the trailer starts to skid, what should you do with the brakes to stop the skid?
choice_a: Release the brakes to let the wheels regain traction
choice_b: Apply the trailer hand brake hard to straighten the rig
choice_c: Pump the foot brake rapidly
choice_d: Apply maximum brake pressure until fully stopped
explanation: The correct procedure is to release the brakes to get traction back; once the trailer wheels grip the road again, the trailer will follow the tractor and straighten out.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Prevent Trailer Skids

question: Why should you never use the trailer hand brake to try to straighten out a jackknifing trailer?
choice_a: Because the brakes on the trailer wheels caused the skid in the first place
choice_b: Because it will drain the air tanks too quickly
choice_c: Because it is illegal to use the hand valve under any circumstance
choice_d: Because it will automatically uncouple the trailer
explanation: The manual explains this is the wrong thing to do since the trailer wheel brakes caused the skid in the first place.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Prevent Trailer Skids

question: A "trailer jackknife" caused by locked-up trailer wheels is more likely to happen when the trailer is:
choice_a: Empty or lightly loaded
choice_b: Fully loaded to maximum weight
choice_c: Carrying liquid cargo only
choice_d: Equipped with ABS on all axles
explanation: The manual notes this type of jackknife, called a trailer jackknife, is more likely when the trailer is empty or lightly loaded.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Prevent Trailer Skids

question: What is "off-tracking" (also called "cheating")?
choice_a: The rear wheels of a vehicle following a different, shorter path than the front wheels around a corner
choice_b: The trailer swinging out during hard braking
choice_c: A tire losing air pressure while turning
choice_d: The tractor drifting into the oncoming lane on a straightaway
explanation: The manual defines off-tracking, or cheating, as the rear wheels following a different path than the front wheels when a vehicle goes around a corner.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Turn Wide

question: In a combination vehicle pulling more than one trailer, which wheels off-track the most during a turn?
choice_a: The rear wheels of the last trailer
choice_b: The rear wheels of the tractor
choice_c: The front wheels of the tractor
choice_d: The wheels of the first trailer only
explanation: The manual states that if there is more than one trailer, the rear wheels of the last trailer will off-track the most.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Turn Wide

question: When turning a corner, why should you keep the rear of your vehicle close to the curb while steering the front end wide?
choice_a: To stop other drivers from passing you on the right
choice_b: To reduce fuel consumption during the turn
choice_c: To keep the trailer brakes from overheating
choice_d: Because it is required for ABS to activate correctly
explanation: The manual explains that keeping the rear close to the curb while steering wide up front will stop other drivers from passing you on the right.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Turn Wide

question: When backing a trailer, which direction do you initially turn the top of the steering wheel compared to backing a car, straight truck, or bus?
choice_a: The opposite direction
choice_b: The same direction
choice_c: It makes no difference which direction
choice_d: Only to the left, regardless of the desired direction
explanation: The manual explains that when backing a trailer you turn the steering wheel in the opposite direction from backing a car, straight truck, or bus.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Backing with a Trailer

question: If you must back a trailer on a curved path, to which side should you back to maintain the best visibility?
choice_a: The driver's side
choice_b: The passenger's side
choice_c: Either side, it makes no difference
choice_d: You should never back on a curved path under any circumstance
explanation: The manual advises that if you must back on a curved path, back to the driver's side so you can see.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Backing with a Trailer

question: Before backing a trailer, what should you do first regarding your intended path of travel?
choice_a: Get out and walk around the vehicle to check your line of travel and clearance
choice_b: Immediately begin backing slowly without checking
choice_c: Rely entirely on a passenger's verbal directions without checking yourself
choice_d: Fold in your outside mirrors to avoid distraction
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to look at their path before beginning, getting out and walking around the vehicle to check clearance to the sides and overhead.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Backing with a Trailer

question: If you notice the trailer drifting off the proper path while backing, what should you do?
choice_a: Correct it immediately by turning the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift
choice_b: Continue backing and correct only once fully stopped
choice_c: Pull forward and restart from a different spot every time
choice_d: Apply the trailer hand valve to stop the drift
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to correct drift immediately by turning the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift, once the drift is seen.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Backing with a Trailer

question: What is another name for the trailer hand valve?
choice_a: The trolley valve or Johnson bar
choice_b: The governor valve
choice_c: The relay valve
choice_d: The quick-release valve
explanation: The manual states the trailer hand valve is also called the trolley valve or Johnson bar.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Hand Valve

question: The trailer hand valve should be used only for what purpose while operating the vehicle?
choice_a: Testing the trailer brakes
choice_b: Normal stopping in traffic
choice_c: Parking on a hill
choice_d: Emergency stops at highway speed
explanation: The manual states the trailer hand valve should be used only to test the trailer brakes, not for driving, because of the danger of making the trailer skid.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Hand Valve

question: Why is it dangerous to use the trailer hand valve for parking a trailer that lacks spring brakes?
choice_a: All the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes
choice_b: It will overheat the brake shoes within minutes
choice_c: It automatically uncouples the trailer from the tractor
choice_d: It triggers the ABS malfunction lamp permanently
explanation: The manual warns never to use the hand valve for parking because all the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes in trailers without spring brakes.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Hand Valve

question: What is the purpose of the tractor protection valve?
choice_a: To keep air in the tractor or truck brake system if the trailer breaks away or develops a bad leak
choice_b: To control the trailer's turn signals
choice_c: To regulate engine RPM during braking
choice_d: To automatically release the trailer's parking brake
explanation: The manual explains the tractor protection valve keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system should the trailer break away or develop a bad leak.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Tractor Protection Valve

question: The tractor protection valve will close automatically when air pressure drops into approximately what range?
choice_a: 20 to 45 psi
choice_b: 60 to 80 psi
choice_c: 5 to 10 psi
choice_d: 100 to 120 psi
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve closes automatically if air pressure is low, in the range of 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Tractor Protection Valve

question: What happens to the trailer emergency brakes when the tractor protection valve closes?
choice_a: They come on, because air is let out of the trailer emergency line
choice_b: They release completely
choice_c: They are unaffected by the tractor protection valve
choice_d: They switch to manual control only
explanation: The manual states that when the tractor protection valve closes, it lets the air out of the trailer emergency line, causing the trailer emergency brakes to come on.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Tractor Protection Valve

question: On newer vehicles, what does pulling out the red eight-sided trailer air supply knob do?
choice_a: Shuts off air to the trailer and applies the trailer emergency brakes
choice_b: Supplies extra air to the service brakes only
choice_c: Releases the parking brakes
choice_d: Disconnects the electrical cord
explanation: The manual states you pull the trailer air supply knob out to shut the air off and put on the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Air Supply Control

question: On older vehicles with a lever instead of a knob for the tractor protection valve control, what is the "normal" position used for?
choice_a: Pulling a trailer
choice_b: Testing the ABS system
choice_c: Uncoupling the trailer
choice_d: Parking the tractor permanently
explanation: The manual notes that on older vehicles the 'normal' position of the lever is used for pulling a trailer, while 'emergency' shuts the air off and applies the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Air Supply Control

question: What are the two air-lines found on every combination vehicle?
choice_a: The service line and the emergency line
choice_b: The primary line and the backup line
choice_c: The hydraulic line and the pneumatic line
choice_d: The parking line and the driving line
explanation: The manual states every combination vehicle has two air-lines, the service line and the emergency line, running between each vehicle in the combination.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Air-lines

question: What does the service air-line (also called the control or signal line) carry?
choice_a: Air controlled by the foot brake or trailer hand valve, with pressure that changes based on how hard the brake is applied
choice_b: A constant, unchanging air pressure at all times
choice_c: Only electrical signals, with no air
choice_d: Fuel for the trailer's auxiliary systems
explanation: The manual describes the service line as carrying air controlled by the foot brake or trailer hand brake, with pressure changing depending on how hard the brake is applied.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Air-lines

question: What are the two purposes of the emergency air-line (also called the supply line)?
choice_a: Supplying air to the trailer air tanks and controlling the trailer emergency brakes
choice_b: Powering the trailer lights and charging the trailer battery
choice_c: Cooling the brake drums and lubricating the fifth wheel
choice_d: Providing backup steering assist and horn power
explanation: The manual states the emergency line first supplies air to the trailer air tanks, and second controls the emergency brakes on combination vehicles.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Air-lines

question: Emergency air-lines are often color-coded with which color, to avoid confusing them with the service line?
choice_a: Red
choice_b: Blue
choice_c: Green
choice_d: Yellow
explanation: The manual states emergency lines are often coded red, to keep from getting them mixed up with the blue service line.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Air-lines

question: What happens if you cross the air-lines when coupling (connect service to emergency and vice versa)?
choice_a: Air will not be available to release the trailer spring brakes, so you would have no trailer brakes
choice_b: The trailer running lights will fail to work
choice_c: The ABS malfunction lamp will flash continuously
choice_d: The system automatically corrects the crossed lines within seconds
explanation: The manual warns that crossing the air-lines sends supply air to the service line instead of charging the trailer air tanks, so air will not be available to release the spring brakes, which is very dangerous.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Air-lines

question: When connecting glad hands, at what angle should the two rubber seals be pressed together before locking them?
choice_a: A 90 degree angle to each other
choice_b: A 180 degree angle
choice_c: A 45 degree angle
choice_d: A 360 degree angle
explanation: The manual instructs pressing the two seals together with the couplers at a 90 degree angle to each other, then turning the glad hand to join and lock the couplers.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: What color is typically used to identify the service line glad hand, as opposed to the emergency line?
choice_a: Blue
choice_b: Red
choice_c: Green
choice_d: Black
explanation: The manual states blue is used for the service lines and red for the emergency (supply) lines to help avoid mistakes during coupling.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: What fills the air tanks on each trailer and converter dolly?
choice_a: The emergency (supply) line from the tractor
choice_b: The service line only
choice_c: A separate onboard compressor on each trailer
choice_d: The electrical cord
explanation: The manual states trailer and dolly air tanks are filled by the emergency (supply) line from the tractor.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Air Tanks

question: Why should you drain water and oil from trailer air tanks every day, even if the tanks have automatic drains?
choice_a: Water and oil buildup can cause the brakes to not work correctly
choice_b: It improves fuel economy on long routes
choice_c: It is required to reset the ABS system
choice_d: It prevents the tires from overinflating
explanation: The manual states it is important not to let water and oil build up in the air tanks because the brakes may not work correctly if you do, and drains should be opened even with automatic drains to make sure.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Air Tanks

question: How should the shut-off valves (cut-out cocks) at the back of the last trailer be positioned when towing another trailer?
choice_a: Closed
choice_b: Fully open at all times regardless of position
choice_c: Removed entirely from the trailer
choice_d: Only the service line needs to be closed, never the emergency line
explanation: The manual states shut-off valves are used in the service and supply air-lines at the back of trailers, and must all be open except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Shut-off Valves

topic: Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes
question: Converter dollies and trailers built before what year are not required to have spring brakes?
explanation: The manual states converter dollies and trailers built before 1975 are not required to have spring brakes.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

topic: Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes
question: Trailers without spring brakes have no parking brake, so what must be used to keep them from moving when parked?
choice_a: Wheel chocks
choice_b: The trailer hand valve left engaged
choice_c: The tractor's parking brake alone, with the trailer disconnected
choice_d: A mechanical drawbar lock
explanation: The manual emphasizes that it is very important for safety to use wheel chocks when parking trailers without spring brakes, since their brakes will only hold as long as air pressure remains.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

topic: Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes
question: On a trailer without spring brakes, what eventually happens to the emergency brakes if air pressure is lost and not restored?
choice_a: The air will leak away and there will be no brakes at all
choice_b: The brakes will lock permanently
choice_c: The brakes automatically switch to a hydraulic backup system
choice_d: The brakes stay applied indefinitely
explanation: The manual explains that these trailers' emergency brakes hold only as long as there is air pressure in the trailer air tank; eventually the air will leak away and there will be no brakes.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

topic: Antilock Brake Systems on Combination Vehicles
question: All trailers and converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have ABS?
choice_a: March 1, 1998
choice_b: January 1, 2000
choice_c: July 1, 1995
choice_d: March 1, 2005
explanation: The manual states all trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have ABS.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Antilock Brake Systems

topic: Antilock Brake Systems on Combination Vehicles
question: Where are ABS malfunction lamps located on trailers required to have the system?
choice_a: Yellow lamps on the left side, either front or rear corner
choice_b: Red lamps on the rear bumper
choice_c: Green lamps near the fifth wheel
choice_d: Blue lamps inside the cab only
explanation: The manual states trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Antilock Brake Systems

topic: Antilock Brake Systems on Combination Vehicles
question: Does ABS decrease or increase a vehicle's normal braking capability?
choice_a: Neither; ABS is an addition to normal brakes and only activates when wheels are about to lock up
choice_b: Yes, it always significantly shortens stopping distance
choice_c: Yes, it roughly doubles normal braking force
choice_d: No, because ABS replaces the normal brakes entirely
explanation: The manual states ABS is an addition to normal brakes; it does not decrease or increase normal braking capability and only activates when wheels are about to lock up.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Antilock Brake Systems

topic: Antilock Brake Systems on Combination Vehicles
question: If only the trailer has ABS and you begin to lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife, what should you do?
choice_a: Let up on the brakes, if you can safely do so, until you regain control
choice_b: Apply the trailer hand valve immediately and hold it
choice_c: Continue braking at full force to stop faster
choice_d: Accelerate to try to regain traction
explanation: The manual advises that when only the trailer has ABS, if you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife, let up on the brakes if you can safely do so until you gain control.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Antilock Brake Systems

topic: Antilock Brake Systems on Combination Vehicles
question: How should you brake differently when driving a tractor-trailer combination equipped with ABS compared to one without it?
choice_a: You should brake the same way regardless of whether you have ABS
choice_b: You should brake much harder since ABS prevents all skids
choice_c: You should pump the brakes rapidly at all times
choice_d: You should rely only on the trailer hand valve
explanation: The manual instructs that when driving with ABS, you should brake as you always have, using only the braking force necessary and braking the same way regardless of whether the tractor, trailer, or both have ABS.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Antilock Brake Systems

question: Before backing the tractor under the trailer to couple, how should the tractor be positioned?
choice_a: Directly in front of the trailer, never at an angle
choice_b: At a 45-degree angle for better mirror visibility
choice_c: As close to the curb as possible
choice_d: With the parking brake released before positioning
explanation: The manual instructs putting the tractor directly in front of the trailer and never backing under it at an angle, because doing so might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: What should the trailer height be, relative to the tractor, before backing the tractor under it?
choice_a: Low enough that it is raised slightly by the tractor when backed under
choice_b: Exactly level with the top of the fifth wheel plate
choice_c: As high as possible to avoid any contact
choice_d: It does not matter as long as the kingpin is visible
explanation: The manual states the trailer should be low enough that it is raised slightly by the tractor when backed under it; if too low the tractor may damage the trailer nose, and if too high it may not couple correctly.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: After supplying air to the trailer brake system during coupling, what should you do before trusting the trailer brakes are working?
choice_a: Shut the engine off, apply and release the trailer brakes, and listen for them to move and air to escape
choice_b: Immediately drive away at normal speed
choice_c: Disconnect the electrical cord to test the brakes independently
choice_d: Skip testing since the ABS lamp will indicate any problem
explanation: The manual instructs shutting the engine off so you can hear the brakes, then applying and releasing trailer brakes and listening for the sound of the brakes being applied and released.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: After the kingpin is locked into the fifth wheel, how do you check the coupling connection for security?
choice_a: Raise the landing gear slightly and pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are locked
choice_b: Immediately raise the landing gear all the way and drive off
choice_c: Only check visually from a distance without moving the tractor
choice_d: Disconnect the air-lines and see if the trailer rolls
explanation: The manual instructs raising the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground, then pulling the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked to check that the trailer is locked onto the tractor.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: When inspecting the completed coupling, what should you check for between the upper and lower fifth wheel?
choice_a: There should be no visible space; if there is, something is wrong
choice_b: There should be a small gap of about one inch
choice_c: The gap should match the tire tread depth
choice_d: This check is unnecessary if the air brakes tested fine
explanation: The manual states there should be no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel; if there is space, something is wrong, possibly the kingpin sitting on top of the closed fifth wheel jaws.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: After raising the landing gear all the way up, what should you do with the crank handle?
choice_a: Secure it safely
choice_b: Leave it hanging freely so it can be seen
choice_c: Remove it from the trailer entirely
choice_d: Lock it in the down position
explanation: The manual instructs securing the crank handle safely after raising the landing gear.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: Before disconnecting the air-lines during uncoupling, why should you chock the trailer wheels if the trailer doesn't have spring brakes?
choice_a: Air could leak out of the trailer air tank, releasing the emergency brakes and allowing the trailer to move
choice_b: It is required only in cold weather conditions
choice_c: It prevents theft of the trailer while unattended
choice_d: It keeps the landing gear from collapsing under load
explanation: The manual instructs chocking the trailer wheels if the trailer doesn't have spring brakes or you're not sure, because air could leak out of the trailer air tank, releasing its emergency brakes.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: When uncoupling, why should you stop with the tractor frame still under the trailer after pulling the fifth wheel partially clear?
choice_a: This prevents the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink
choice_b: It allows you to check tire pressure more easily
choice_c: It is required so the ABS system can reset
choice_d: It makes reconnecting the electrical cord easier
explanation: The manual instructs stopping with the tractor frame under the trailer to prevent the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers

topic: Coupling and Uncoupling a Pintle Hook
question: What could result if a pintle hook is not properly secured to its mounting surface before operating the vehicle?
choice_a: The pintle hook could separate from the vehicle, resulting in death or serious injury
choice_b: The trailer lights would fail to illuminate
choice_c: The ABS malfunction lamp would illuminate
choice_d: Fuel efficiency would decrease slightly
explanation: The manual warns that if the pintle hook is not secured to the mounting surface, it could separate from the vehicle, which if not avoided could result in death or serious injury.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Coupling a Pintle Hook

topic: Coupling and Uncoupling a Pintle Hook
question: When a pintle hook is correctly locked after coupling, what happens to the lock handle?
choice_a: It rotates and moves up until it is flush with the top of the latch
choice_b: It disappears into the hook body entirely
choice_c: It turns bright red as a visual indicator
choice_d: It automatically disconnects the safety chains
explanation: The manual states that when correctly locked, the lock handle will rotate and move up until it is flush with the top of the latch.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Coupling a Pintle Hook

topic: Coupling and Uncoupling a Pintle Hook
question: When uncoupling a trailer at a pintle hook, what must you check about the ground surface before extending the trailer jack?
choice_a: That the ground surface below the jack pad will support the tongue load
choice_b: That the ground is painted with a designated parking marker
choice_c: That the ground is level with the roadway shoulder
choice_d: That the ground has been inspected by a mechanic
explanation: The manual instructs checking that the ground surface below the jack pad will support the tongue load before extending the jack when uncoupling a pintle hook trailer.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Uncoupling a Pintle Hook

question: During a walk-around inspection of a combination vehicle's fifth wheel, the locking jaws should be closed around what part of the kingpin?
choice_a: The shank, not the head, of the kingpin
choice_b: The head, not the shank, of the kingpin
choice_c: Either the head or the shank, it does not matter
choice_d: The kingpin does not need to be checked if air pressure is normal
explanation: The manual instructs checking that the locking jaws are around the shank, not the head, of the kingpin.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Inspecting a Combination Vehicle

question: What should you check regarding the fifth wheel's position relative to the tractor during inspection?
choice_a: That it is not so far forward that the tractor frame will hit the landing gear or the cab will hit the trailer during turns
choice_b: That it is positioned as far forward as physically possible
choice_c: That it is left unlocked for easy on-road adjustment
choice_d: That the glide plate has been removed for the inspection
explanation: The manual instructs checking that the fifth wheel is not so far forward that the tractor frame will hit the landing gear, or the cab will hit the trailer, during turns.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Inspecting a Combination Vehicle

question: When checking that air flows to all trailers, what confirms the entire system is charged after opening the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer?
choice_a: Hearing air escaping
choice_b: Complete silence at the valve
choice_c: A clicking sound from the ABS sensor
choice_d: The engine idling down
explanation: The manual states you should hear air escaping at the rear shut-off valve, showing the entire system is charged.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Combination Vehicle Brake Check

question: To test the tractor protection valve, after building normal air pressure and shutting off the engine, what should you do?
choice_a: Step on and off the brake pedal several times to reduce air pressure and watch for the control to pop out
choice_b: Immediately drive the vehicle at highway speed
choice_c: Disconnect the emergency line and observe the trailer
choice_d: Apply only the trailer hand valve repeatedly
explanation: The manual instructs stepping on and off the brake pedal several times to reduce air pressure in the tanks, checking that the trailer air supply control pops out within the manufacturer's specified range.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Combination Vehicle Brake Check

question: To test the trailer service brakes, after checking for normal air pressure and releasing the parking brakes, what do you do?
choice_a: Move the vehicle forward slowly and apply the trailer brakes with the hand control to feel them engage
choice_b: Slam on the foot brake while at highway speed
choice_c: Disconnect the air-lines and observe the brake response
choice_d: Rely solely on the ABS malfunction lamp
explanation: The manual instructs moving the vehicle forward slowly and applying trailer brakes with the hand control (trolley valve) to feel the brakes come on, confirming they are connected and working.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Combination Vehicle Brake Check

question: To test the trailer emergency brakes, after charging the trailer air brake system and checking that the trailer rolls freely, what do you do?
choice_a: Pull out the trailer air supply control (or place it in the emergency position) and pull gently on the trailer with the tractor
choice_b: Immediately release the parking brake and accelerate hard
choice_c: Disconnect the electrical cord and observe the brake lights
choice_d: Push the trailer air supply knob in fully and drive forward at normal speed
explanation: The manual instructs pulling out the trailer air supply control or placing it in the emergency position, then pulling gently on the trailer with the tractor to check that the emergency brakes come on.
source_note: Louisiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Louisiana DPS/OMV -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, Combination Vehicle Brake Check
